lesson.title: The -ir & -re Verb Bridges
lesson.subtitle: finir (finish), choisir (choose), vendre (vendor), répondre (respond) — French's other two verb families

hook.title: Where English -ish Came From
hook.content: Over 80% of French verbs end in -er, which you unlock via -ation. The remaining verbs live in two smaller houses: -ir verbs (like finir 'to finish' and choisir 'to choose') and -re verbs (like vendre 'to sell', répondre 'to respond', and attendre 'to wait for'). Why does English say 'finish', 'punish', and 'abolish' with -ish? Because French -ir verbs insert -iss- in the plural (nous finissons), and Norman English borrowed that exact stem!

footnotes.title: The Norman -iss- that became English -ish
footnotes.content: Latin had an 'inchoative' infix -isc- meaning 'to begin to'. French generalized it across -ir plurals (finissons, choisissons), and Middle English adopted that stem as -ish: finir → finish, punir → punish.

pattern.title: Same Infinitive Slot After je veux
pattern.content: Whether a verb ends in -er (confirmer), -ir (finir, choisir), or -re (vendre, répondre, attendre), it parks unchanged right after je veux or tu veux: Je veux finir le café. Tu veux choisir le gâteau. Ils veulent vendre la maison. You already know the meanings from English finish, choose, vendor, and respond.
pattern.linguist_note: French's three conjugation classes (-er, -ir, -re) descend from Latin's four (-āre, -ēre/-īre, -ere). In infinitive chains after vouloir, all three behave identically.
pattern.trap_note: Your mind will try to add 'for' after attendre ('wait for') or 'to' after répondre in English order. Remember: attendre already means 'to wait for' inside one word!

exercises.prompt: Match each -ir or -re infinitive with its English cognate and meaning:
exercises.meaning: to finish (English finish), to choose (English choose), to sell (English vendor), to answer (English respond), to wait for (false friend: attend)
exercises.explanation: English -ish verbs map to French -ir; Latinate -nd verbs map to French -re.

exercises.prompt: Assemble 'I want to finish the coffee':
exercises.explanation: finir parks in its dictionary form right after je veux.

exercises.prompt: Which English noun for a person or machine that sells things shares the root of French vendre?
exercises.explanation: Latin vendere gave French vendre and English vendor / vending machine.

exercises.idea: you are asking a friend if they want to choose the cake
exercises.meaning: Do you want to choose the cake?
exercises.explanation: Tu veux choisir le gâteau chains the -ir infinitive directly after veux.

diagnosis.cue: Keep choisir in its bare -ir infinitive form after tu veux.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.explanation: répondre drops the Latin s before p and marks the spot with an acute accent é.
exercises.affirmation: You caught répondre with its é and final -re.

summary.outcome: Decode -ir verbs from English -ish cognates (finish → finir) and -re verbs from Latinate stems (vendor → vendre, respond → répondre).

use_example.german: Je veux finir mon café et choisir un gâteau.
use_example.english: I want to finish my coffee and choose a cake.

summary.takeaway: English -ish verbs are French -ir verbs in disguise, and they chain after je veux just like -er verbs.

twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Tu veux choisir le gâteau" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of The -ir & -re Verb Bridges.

finir.context_translation: I want to finish my coffee.
finir.etymology_derivation: French 2nd conjugation (-ir) extended plurals with -iss- (nous finissons), which English borrowed as -ish: finish, punish, abolish.

choisir.context_translation: You are going to choose the cake.
choisir.etymology_derivation: Frankish *kausjan (cousin of English choose) entered French as an -ir verb.

vendre.context_translation: They want to sell the house.
vendre.etymology_derivation: Latin vendere — English kept it in vendor and vending machine.

répondre.etymology_derivation: Latin respondēre 'to pledge back'. Notice the dropped s turns into the acute accent on é.

attendre.context_translation: I am waiting for the train.
attendre.etymology_derivation: Latin attendere 'to stretch toward'. In French it means to wait for — with no preposition 'for' needed!

vouloir.etymology_derivation: Latin volō 'I want' → vouloir. A volunteer is the one who wants to do — the want-root English kept in voluntary, benevolent.

café.etymology_derivation: Turkish kahve → Italian caffè → French café. English took the same journey twice: coffee and café.

maison.etymology_derivation: Latin mansiō 'a staying' → maison and mansion: the house you stay in, and the big one.

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.
